summary: This unit teaches you how a manager finds a business opportunity, tests it and then acts on it before the chance is gone. You will learn to screen ideas, use SWOT, PESTLE, the five forces and the Ansoff matrix, test demand cheaply, check the numbers (break-even, margin of safety, payback and return on investment), manage risk and legal points, find money, people and partners, launch within about 90 days, and monitor, adjust or stop the venture.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. It is written for supervisors and managers in Jamaican businesses, hotels, schools and public bodies who must decide whether to act on a new opportunity and then carry it through. A good opportunity can be lost in a few weeks if the manager is slow, and a bad one can cost a business its savings. The skill is to move quickly **on evidence**, with risks that you have measured and limited.

An **opportunity** is a gap or need that your organisation can meet at a profit (or, for a public or community body, with a worthwhile result for the money spent). An opportunity is not just a good idea: it needs customers who will pay, a margin that covers the cost, and an organisation able to deliver it in time.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Spot openings in changes in the economy, law, technology, society and the environment, and in customer problems and gaps left by rivals.
Test ideas against demand, profit, fit with the organisation, risk and timing, and rank them with a weighted score.
Use SWOT, PESTLE, the five forces, the Ansoff matrix and a competitor check to see how strong the opportunity really is.
Use trials, pilots, pre-orders and a simple first version before committing large sums.
Work out contribution, break-even, margin of safety, profit, payback and return on investment, and allow for opportunity cost and the cash gap.
Manage risk, legal and ethical points
Rate risks, limit the money at stake, set an exit point, and check licences, registrations, standards, employment and data rules.
Match the right kind of finance to the need, bring in people on clear terms, and use partners and networks.
Write an action plan with owners and milestones, set the price and message, and lead staff through the change.
Compare results with targets, change the offer when customers tell you to, stop at the agreed exit point, and record the lessons.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** with scenario and calculation questions, such as break-even, payback and weighted scores.
A **written paper** of short answers (exact terms such as pivot, sunk cost, USP) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Practical group work**: screening three opportunities and choosing one, then planning a 90-day launch and pitching it to a panel. Each member takes a named role and the assessor checks that sums were done carefully and checked twice.

blocks.note: Learn the formulas in the section on the numbers and practise them with your own J$ figures. Most marks are lost by using the wrong formula or by mixing up contribution and profit.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Many people have ideas. Few ideas are opportunities. The test is whether real customers will pay enough, often enough, for the organisation to make a profit, and whether the organisation can deliver.

head: An idea only
A real opportunity
rows: The owner likes it and is excited
Customers have a need and say so by their actions
Friends and family say it is clever
Enough customers will pay at a price that gives a profit
Costs are known and the margin covers them
It would be fun to run
It fits the organisation's skills, money and goals
The timing is right: the window is open now

blocks.note: Nobody having tried something before is **not** evidence of an opportunity. It can mean there is no demand. Equally, a product a rival already sells well is not automatically an opportunity for you unless you can serve the market better or in a different place.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Source
Examples in Jamaica
rows: More money sent home by Jamaicans abroad, more visitors, a change in the exchange rate that makes local goods cheaper for buyers overseas
Rules that limit some single-use plastics (a market for reusable packaging); tax or investment incentives for a sector; new standards that many firms must meet
Mobile payments, online ordering, delivery apps, solar equipment, cheaper machinery
Working parents who need after-school care, an ageing population, healthier eating, more remote workers
A new highway that shortens travel times and makes day trips and new delivery routes possible
Drought and storms that create demand for water storage, irrigation and stronger buildings
Repeated complaints, requests nobody meets, a rival that closes or raises prices
Spare capacity, by-products or waste that could be sold, skills your staff already have

blocks.p: A manager should **scan** these sources regularly, not only when the business is in trouble. Staff who meet customers every day, such as sales staff and drivers, often hear the first signs.

ol: **Demand:** who exactly are the customers, how many are there, and will they pay this price?
**Profit:** after all the costs, is the margin worth the effort and the risk?
**Fit:** does it suit our goals, skills, equipment and brand?
**Resources:** can we find the money, people and time without damaging the core business?
**Risk:** what could go wrong, how badly, and can we limit the loss?
**Timing:** how long will the window stay open, and how long do we need to get ready?
**Legal and ethical:** are we allowed to do this, and would we be proud to explain how we did it?
**Growth:** can sales rise without costs rising as fast?

blocks.p: If an opportunity is far from the firm's skills, such as a computer repair shop asked to supply hotel uniforms, ask first whether it fits the firm's skills, resources and goals. A profitable-looking offer that needs skills you do not have usually costs more than it earns.

When there are several opportunities and resources for only one, give each a score against the same criteria. Because some criteria matter more, give each a **weight** (the weights add up to 100%). Multiply each score by its weight and add up.

Option Y ranks higher (7.1 against 6.9). Check the sum twice: 3.6 + 1.5 + 1.4 + 0.6 = 7.1. The matrix does not decide for you. The scores are judgements, so a close result means you need better evidence, and you should test what happens to the ranking if one weight changes.

blocks.h: Timing and the window of opportunity

blocks.p: A **window of opportunity** is the limited time in which an opportunity can be taken: a large event, a contract offer, a gap left by a rival that has closed, or a grant scheme with a closing date. A manager who waits for perfect information may see the window close.

head: Point
Being first to market
Waiting and following
rows: Win loyal customers before rivals arrive
Secure the best sites, partners and suppliers
Can charge more while there is little competition
Learn from the first firm's mistakes
Time to build a better product
Cost of teaching customers about a new product
Weak evidence; costs and demand may be misjudged
Rivals copy the idea and may do it better
Rivals may have won the loyal customers
The best partners and sites may be gone

blocks.note: When the window is short, decide promptly on the evidence you hold, test what you can cheaply, and act in stages. Speed with evidence beats speed without it, and it beats delay.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Analysis tools do not give answers. They organise what you know and show what you still need to find out.
A SWOT analysis sorts facts into four boxes. The test is simple: **is the factor inside the organisation or outside it?**

head: Where
Helpful
Harmful
rows: **Strengths**: skilled staff, a good location, a loyal customer base, cash in the bank
**Weaknesses**: little cash for stock, no experience in the new area, old equipment
**Opportunities**: a new incentive, rising demand, a rival closing, a new highway
**Threats**: a new competitor, rising fuel prices, new rules, falling demand

blocks.p: Strengths and weaknesses are internal. Opportunities and threats are external. A tax incentive for agro-processing is an opportunity; a rival's free-delivery offer is a threat; a lack of cash is a weakness. Use the SWOT to build strategy: use strengths to take opportunities, and fix or work round weaknesses before the threats find them.
PESTLE is a checklist of outside factors. Work through all six.

head: Letter
Factor
Example
rows: Government policy, incentives, trade agreements, elections
Remittances, exchange rate, interest rates, fuel and energy costs, household spending
Population change, lifestyles, tastes, working patterns
Mobile payments, online ordering, new equipment
Licences, standards, employment law, data protection law, rules on packaging and labelling
Weather, hurricanes, drought, waste rules, climate

blocks.p: Michael Porter's model asks how attractive an industry is, by looking at five pressures on profit.

ul: **Rivalry** among existing firms (many equal rivals usually means price cutting).
**Threat of new entrants** (low start-up cost and few licences make entry easy and profits harder to defend).
**Threat of substitutes** (a different product that meets the same need, such as a bus ride instead of a taxi).
**Bargaining power of buyers** (a few large customers can demand low prices).
**Bargaining power of suppliers** (a single supplier of a key input can raise prices).

blocks.p: Igor Ansoff's matrix sorts growth strategies by whether the product and the market are existing or new. Risk rises as you move away from what you already know.

head: Market
Existing product
New product
rows: **Market penetration**: sell more of the same product to the same customers
**Product development**: a new product for the same customers
**Market development**: the same product to new customers or places (for example, selling an existing product to another country)
**Diversification**: a new product for a new market

blocks.note: A Montego Bay bakery that sells its existing bun and cheese to shops in another country is market development. If the same bakery started to run a tour business, that would be diversification.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Know your competitors and your difference

blocks.p: Study rivals using public information: their prices, services, locations, customer reviews and gaps. Do not use dishonest methods such as pretending to be a customer to get private information. Then state your **USP** (unique selling point): the feature that makes your offer different and worth choosing, such as speed, quality, location, price or a service nobody else gives. Name the **target market**: the particular group of customers you aim to sell to. A USP that no customer cares about is not a USP.
The cheapest mistake is the one you find before you invest. Before you buy equipment or hire staff, test whether customers will really buy at your price and whether you can deliver at your cost.

head: Evidence
How strong
Why
rows: They want to be kind and do not pay
A survey saying "I would probably buy"
People overstate what they will do; treat it as an upper limit
Shows interest, but no money has changed hands
Repeat purchases at the full price
Customers came back and paid again

ul: **Trial sale or pop-up:** sell a small batch at a market stall, a trade fair or in a few outlets and record the results.
**Minimum viable product (MVP):** a simple first version with only the essential features, used to test real demand and learn from real users before the full version is built.
**Pilot:** run the whole service on a small scale, in one area or for one client, with a target set in advance.
**Pre-orders and deposits:** ask real customers to commit money before you produce.
**Customer interviews:** short, open questions about problems and current spending. They show needs, but not how many will buy.

blocks.p: Set a **target before the test** (for example, "at least 30 pre-orders at J$2,500"). If you decide what counts as success afterwards, you will always find a reason to carry on.

blocks.h: What to do with the results

ul: **Go:** results meet or beat the target and the numbers still work.
**Adjust:** customers like the idea but not part of it, such as the price, size or flavour. Change that part and test again.
**Pivot:** a change of direction based on what you learned from customers, such as selling a related product they keep asking for.
**Stop:** results are far below target and no adjustment looks likely to fix them.

blocks.note: Stopping early after a cheap test is a success: you kept your money for a better opportunity. Money already spent that cannot be recovered is a **sunk cost** and must not push you to carry on.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: An opportunity must pass the numbers test. Work every calculation twice, and write down the assumptions behind it, such as the price, the number of customers and the cost per unit.

head: Term
Formula
Meaning
rows: Selling price − variable cost per unit
What each sale adds towards fixed costs and profit
The sales at which total income equals total costs: no profit, no loss
How far sales can fall before a loss begins (often shown as a percentage of expected sales)
Profit at the expected level of sales
Cost of investment ÷ net cash gained each year
How long to get the investment back
Net profit (or net gain) ÷ cost of investment × 100
The percentage return each year on the money put in

blocks.note: **Fixed costs** do not change with output in the short term (rent, insurance, loan payments). **Variable costs** change with each unit sold (ingredients, fuel, packaging). Never use total cost per unit to work out break-even.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Selling price J$450 a cup; variable cost (fruit, cup, sugar) J$270 a cup; fixed costs J$162,000 a month; expected sales 1,200 cups a month.

ol: Margin of safety = 1,200 − 900 = **300 cups**, which is 300 ÷ 1,200 = 25% of expected sales.
Expected profit = (1,200 × 180) − 162,000 = 216,000 − 162,000 = **J$54,000** a month. Check: 300 cups above break-even × J$180 = J$54,000.

blocks.p: A margin of safety of 25% means sales can fall by a quarter before the stand makes a loss. A thin margin of safety means more risk.
A tour van costs J$3,600,000 and is expected to give J$900,000 net cash a year, and net profit of J$540,000 a year after the van's wear and tear.

ul: Simple payback = 3,600,000 ÷ 900,000 = **4 years**.

blocks.p: Payback is easy to understand, but it ignores what happens after the payback date and the timing of cash. If two opportunities have similar profit but one needs J$2 million and the other J$8 million, other things equal the one needing less money carries less risk.

head: Term
Meaning
Example
rows: The benefit given up by choosing one option instead of the next best
A firm uses its only van for a new service and loses J$60,000 a month of normal deliveries: the opportunity cost is J$60,000 a month
Money already spent that cannot be recovered
J$200,000 already spent on a study. It should not decide the new choice

blocks.p: A profitable contract can still bankrupt a firm if the cash goes out before it comes in. Suppose a firm must pay suppliers and staff within 30 days but the customer pays 60 days after delivery. The firm must find the money for the gap. Always draw a **month-by-month cash flow forecast** for a new opportunity, not only a profit sum.
Test the sums with worse figures: sales 10% lower, a price cut, costs 10% higher. If the venture only works when everything goes right, it is too risky as it stands.

blocks.note: Work in GCT 'at the current rate' where it applies. Show prices before GCT in your sums, and remember that GCT collected is owed to the tax authority, not income for the firm.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Managing risk, legal and ethical points

blocks.p: Seizing an opportunity means accepting some risk. Good managers take **calculated** risks: they know what could go wrong, they limit the loss, and they decide in advance when to stop.

head: Risk
Likelihood
Impact
Response
rows: Customers do not buy at the planned price
Reduce: pilot test first; start small
Costs of imported inputs rise with the exchange rate
Reduce: quote in advance; keep a small reserve
Cash runs short because customers pay late
Reduce: deposits, stage payments, short-term finance arranged beforehand
Accident or damage on the job
Accept and prepare: build loyalty and a brand

blocks.p: The four usual responses are to **avoid** the risk (do not do it), **reduce** it (make it less likely or smaller), **transfer** it (insurance or a partner takes it) and **accept** it (with a plan). Give each main risk an owner and review the list regularly in a risk register.

ul: **Start small:** a pilot or one site before the full roll-out.
**Invest in stages:** release more money only when the target for the stage is met.
**Keep a reserve** for surprises.

**Set an exit point before you start:** an agreed level of results (for example, weekly sales below a stated figure after six months) at which you stop. Deciding in advance prevents emotion and sunk costs from keeping you in a losing venture.

blocks.p: Refer to the law by its purpose and confirm the exact requirements with the responsible agency or a qualified adviser. A manager does not need to know every rule, but must know which questions to ask.

head: Check
What to find out
rows: Whether a new company or business name must be registered, under company law, and who the owners and directors are
Whether the venture must register for tax, including GCT where it applies, and for payroll deductions if it will employ staff
Whether the activity needs a licence or permit, for example for food, passenger transport, tourism services, building or alcohol
Product safety, food safety approvals, and the labelling rules for what you sell
Whether the name is already a trade mark, and whether to register your own name and protect your recipe or design
Contracts, pay, hours, safe working conditions and statutory deductions for any new staff
The data protection law: collect only what you need, get consent, store it safely
Written terms with customers, suppliers and partners; the cover the venture needs
Permits and effects on land, water and waste, for example for a quarry or a processing plant

blocks.note: If the team cannot answer a tax or company-law question, seek advice from a qualified adviser, such as an accountant or attorney, before committing money.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: An opportunity that makes quick money by misleading customers, for example about where a product comes from, is **dishonest and unlawful**: reject it. Do not copy a competitor's confidential information, do not hide risks from partners or lenders, and do not accept or offer improper payments. Profit that depends on a lie ends when the lie is found out.

sections.title: Finding the money, people and partners

blocks.p: Seizing an opportunity often needs more than the business has today. The manager's task is to work out exactly what is needed, when, and then to match it to the right source.

blocks.h: Money: match the finance to the need

head: Need
Suitable finance
Notes
rows: A short gap between paying costs and being paid
Overdraft increase, short-term trade or order finance from a bank, invoice finance, customer deposits, longer supplier credit
Backed by a confirmed order or contract; repaid when the customer pays
Equipment or a vehicle that lasts years
A term loan, a lease, or the owners' own capital
Repay over the life of the asset
A bigger venture with high risk
Partners or investors who share ownership
Gives up part of the control and profit
Own savings, a credit union or microfinance loan, development agency support for suitable projects
Check the interest, fees and conditions

blocks.note: Never use short-term money for a long-term asset, or the loan falls due before the asset has earned the cash to repay it.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Compare the **cost** of finance (interest and fees) with the extra profit the opportunity brings. If the cost is higher than the gain, the opportunity is not worth taking on that finance.

ul: Check whether the current team has the skills and the time; asking staff to cover everything may hurt the core business.
Use **overtime** carefully for a short period, and not so much that tired staff make mistakes or leave.
Hire **temporary or contract staff** on clear written terms: duties, pay, hours and the end date.
Bring in **specialists** for particular tasks, and train existing staff in the new skills.

head: Arrangement
What it is
Use it when
rows: Two firms share resources, risk and profit for a particular project
You need skills or capital that the other firm has
An existing outlet or distributor sells your product
You lack an outlet, for example a craft maker who has no shop in a tourist town
Another firm does part of the work for you
A large order is more than your own capacity

blocks.p: Partnerships should be written down: who does what, who pays what, how profit is shared, how to settle disagreements and how to end the arrangement. **Business networks**, such as trade associations, chambers of commerce and trade fairs, bring early news, contacts and possible partners, but they do not replace research and they cannot guarantee finance.
Once an opportunity is approved, the work is to turn the decision into a plan with names and dates, and to bring the people with you.

An **action plan** states, for each key task, the owner, the deadline and the resources. A **milestone** is a key point showing that a stage is complete. A **Gantt chart** shows the tasks as horizontal bars across a timeline on one page, so the order, the timing and any overlaps are clear.

flow: Weeks 1 to 2: appoint a launch leader, confirm the objectives and the budget, and complete the legal and permit checks
Weeks 3 to 6: secure supplies, equipment and premises, recruit and train staff, set prices and prepare the order and payment systems
Weeks 5 to 8: define the target market and the message, prepare materials, and run a pilot with a clear target
Weeks 9 to 12: launch, track results every week against the targets, and fix problems quickly

head: Pricing method
What it means
When it suits
rows: A low introductory price to win customers quickly
A new service in a market with many rivals; plan the later rise
A high price for a unique product, lowered later as rivals appear
A new product that is clearly different and has little competition
A safe minimum; check it against what customers will pay

blocks.p: Choose launch activities that reach your target market at low cost. For young adults in a town, targeted social media posts usually give more reach per J$ than a newspaper advert in a rural weekly paper. Whatever the channel, state the **USP** and the offer clearly and tell customers what to do next.

ul: Explain **why** the opportunity is being taken and how it helps the organisation and the staff.
**Involve** staff in the planning: they often know the practical problems first.
Make roles clear and give training before the launch.
Keep the information flowing: a surprise announcement on launch day, or secrecy, creates rumours and resistance.

blocks.note: Do not ask staff to fund an opportunity from their own pay. Pay and conditions follow employment law and the contracts already agreed.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A launch is the start of the learning, not the end of the work. In the first months, results will differ from the plan. The manager's job is to notice quickly, find the reason, and choose the right response.

ul: Sales volume and value against the target and against break-even.
Gross margin and costs against the budget.
Cash position and the days customers take to pay.
Number of customers, repeat purchases and referrals.
Customer feedback, complaints, and delivery or quality problems.

blocks.p: Review **weekly** in the first months and then monthly. Compare **actual** results with the **plan's targets**; do not rely on how busy the staff feel, or on social media likes alone. Variance is the difference between actual and target. For example, if the target is 30 pick-ups a week and 21 are made, the shortfall is 9, which is 30% of the target (9 ÷ 30 = 0.3).

blocks.h: Decide: grow, adjust, hold or stop

head: Situation
Sensible response
rows: Results beat targets and demand is steady
Grow: add capacity in stages, keeping the checks that worked
Sales are below target, but customers ask for something related
Adjust or pivot: test the related offer with a few customers
Results are below target but above the exit point
Hold: keep trying agreed changes and keep reviewing
Results fall below the agreed exit point
Stop in an orderly way: pay suppliers and staff properly, record the lessons

blocks.note: Do not close a venture at the first poor month, and do not carry on because the money is already spent. Use the targets and the exit point agreed at the start.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: When a venture ends, or at the end of a set period, hold a review. Its purpose is **learning lessons for the next opportunity**, not finding someone to blame. Ask: what did we expect, what happened, why, and what will we do differently? Record the answers, keep the records, and share them with the people who will screen the next idea.

ul: define a business opportunity and explain how it differs from an idea.
name sources of opportunity and use them to scan for openings.
screen opportunities with demand, profit, fit, resources, risk, timing and legal questions, and rank them with a weighted score.
explain a window of opportunity and the advantages and risks of being first to market.
sort points into a SWOT and a PESTLE, and use five forces and the Ansoff matrix.
test demand at low cost and rate how strong the evidence is.
calculate contribution, break-even, margin of safety, profit, payback and ROI, and check each twice.
explain opportunity cost, sunk cost and the cash gap.
rate risks, limit the money at stake and set an exit point.
list the legal and ethical checks before a launch.
match finance to the need and bring in people and partners on clear terms.
write an action plan with owners, deadlines and milestones, and plan a 90-day launch.
monitor results against targets and decide whether to grow, adjust, hold or stop.
carry out a review and record lessons.

terms: A gap or need that an organisation can meet at a profit and in time.
The limited time in which an opportunity can be taken.
Strengths and weaknesses (inside) and opportunities and threats (outside).
A checklist of political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental factors.
Growth options: market penetration, market development, product development, diversification.
Unique selling point: the feature that makes an offer different from rivals' offers.
The particular group of customers a venture aims to sell to.
A simple first version used to test real demand.
A change of direction based on what has been learned from customers.
Selling price less variable cost per unit.
The level of sales at which total income equals total costs.
Cost of the investment divided by the net cash gained each year.
Net profit divided by the money invested, as a percentage.
The benefit given up by choosing one option instead of the next best.

c1.title: Sunset boat trips at Treasure Beach
c1.text: Ricardo Spence owns a fishing boat at Treasure Beach, St Elizabeth. Guest houses ask him for sunset trips for visitors. He plans to charge J$7,500 a guest. Fuel, drinks and the guide's fee cost J$2,500 a guest. Fixed costs (boat loan, insurance, licence and maintenance) are J$180,000 a month. He expects 60 guests a month. A canopy and safety gear will cost a one-off J$1,800,000, which is not in the fixed costs.

c2.title: A big order for a May Pen bakery
c2.text: Shanice Brown runs a bakery in May Pen. A catering contractor offers her an order worth J$2,400,000, delivered in month 1 and paid 60 days after delivery. Flour, packaging and temporary staff will cost J$1,500,000, paid during month 1. Shanice has J$400,000 in the bank and her four bakers are already busy with normal orders.

c3.title: Cocoa and chocolate at Hope Bay
c3.text: Yvonne Mitchell grows cocoa near Hope Bay, Portland, and sells dried beans to a local buyer. She is considering two options: (A) selling her dried beans to a buyer in another country, or (B) making chocolate bars for visitors. At a weekend market she gave out 100 sample bars. She received 35 pre-orders with deposits for gift boxes, but many tasters said the bars were too sweet.

c4.title: Solar water heaters in Old Harbour
c4.text: Kenroy Thomas runs a plumbing and electrical repair firm in Old Harbour, St Catherine. Households are looking for ways to cut electricity bills, so he is thinking of selling and fitting solar water heaters. His two fitters are already trained in plumbing and electrical work. He cannot afford to hold much imported stock, and a rival offers free fitting. If his two fitters work on solar jobs, they cannot do the repair work that earns the firm about J$240,000 a month. He is comparing solar heaters with security cameras, using weights of demand 40%, profit 30%, fit 20% and low risk 10%. Solar heaters score 8, 6, 7 and 5; cameras score 6, 7, 8 and 7.

c5.title: A laundry pick-up service in Ocho Rios
c5.text: Anya McKenzie launched a laundry pick-up service for small guest houses in Ocho Rios, St Ann. Her 90-day target was 30 pick-ups a week, averaging J$9,000 each. After 12 weeks she is doing 21 pick-ups a week. Several guest houses have asked her to add ironing and folding. Before launching, she agreed an exit point: close if weekly sales are below J$150,000 after six months. She is disappointed and wants to stop now.

questions.q: What is Ricardo's contribution for each guest?
questions.why: Contribution is the selling price less the variable cost per unit: 7,500 − 2,500 = J$5,000. It is the amount each guest adds towards fixed costs and profit.

questions.q: How many guests a month must Ricardo carry to break even on his running costs?
o: 24 guests
60 guests
72 guests
36 guests
questions.why: Break-even = fixed costs ÷ contribution = 180,000 ÷ 5,000 = 36 guests. Using the variable cost of J$2,500 by mistake would give 72, which is wrong.

questions.q: If he gets his expected 60 guests, what is his margin of safety?
o: 24 guests, which is 40% of expected sales
36 guests, which is 60% of expected sales
60 guests, which is 100% of expected sales
12 guests, which is 20% of expected sales
questions.why: Margin of safety = expected sales − break-even = 60 − 36 = 24 guests. As a share of expected sales it is 24 ÷ 60 = 40%, so sales can fall by 40% before he makes a loss.

questions.q: At 60 guests a month, how long will the J$1,800,000 canopy and safety gear take to pay back from the monthly profit?
o: 6 months
10 months
15 months
36 months
questions.why: Monthly profit = (60 × 5,000) − 180,000 = J$120,000. Payback = 1,800,000 ÷ 120,000 = 15 months. Dividing by the contribution (300,000) would ignore the fixed costs and give 6 months, which is wrong.

questions.q: What should Shanice do first before she accepts the order?
o: Order all the flour at once to lock in the price
Advertise for permanent bakers to join her team
Draw up a cash flow forecast for the order
Decline the order because her bank balance is small
questions.why: A large order can fail on cash even when it is profitable. A cash flow forecast shows how much is needed and when, so she can arrange money and staff before she commits.

questions.q: How much extra money does she need to find for month 1, on these figures alone?
questions.why: Costs of J$1,500,000 must be paid in month 1 and she has J$400,000. 1,500,000 − 400,000 = J$1,100,000. She is not paid until 60 days after delivery. Check: 400,000 + 1,100,000 = 1,500,000.

questions.q: Which finance best suits this need?
o: A ten-year bank loan to pay for new baking ovens
Asking her bakers to wait for their pay until the contractor pays
Selling a share of the bakery to an outside investor
Short-term bank finance backed by the signed order
questions.why: The need is a temporary gap that closes when the contractor pays, so short-term finance backed by the confirmed order fits. A long loan or new owners are too costly and permanent, and unpaid staff breaks employment obligations.

questions.q: The order needs more people for one month. What is the sensible way to cover it?
o: Ask the four bakers to work double shifts all month
Take on temporary staff on clear written terms
Hire three more bakers permanently from today
Pass part of the work to another bakery with no written agreement
questions.why: Temporary staff meet a one-off peak without adding permanent costs. Overstretched staff make mistakes, permanent hiring commits money after the order ends, and sub-contracting needs written terms for quality and price.

questions.q: Making chocolate bars for visitors, when Yvonne now sells dried beans to a local buyer, is which Ansoff strategy?
o: Product development
Diversification
Market development
Market penetration
questions.why: Chocolate bars are a new product and visitors are a new market. New product plus new market is diversification, which usually carries the highest risk.

questions.q: Selling her existing dried beans to a buyer in another country is which Ansoff strategy?
o: Market penetration
Product development
Market development
Diversification
questions.why: The product stays the same but the market is new, which is market development. It is usually less risky than diversification because she already knows the product.

questions.q: Which result from the market stall is the strongest evidence of demand for the bars?
o: 35 pre-orders with deposits for gift boxes
100 people tasted the sample bars
Shoppers saying the bars looked attractive
The market organiser's view that the bars will sell
questions.why: Pre-orders with deposits show that real customers have committed money. Tasting and compliments cost the customer nothing, so they are weaker evidence.

questions.q: Many tasters said the bars were too sweet. What should Yvonne do?
o: Ignore it, because the pre-orders already prove demand
Stop the project, because the first test did not fully succeed
Buy a full chocolate-making line now to cut the unit cost
Adjust the recipe and test a small new batch
questions.why: Customer feedback on one feature is a reason to adjust and re-test cheaply, not to quit or to spend heavily. Pre-orders were placed on the first recipe, so repeat orders may depend on the fix.

questions.q: Which item belongs under Weakness in Kenroy's SWOT?
o: Households are looking for ways to cut electricity bills
A rival offers free fitting
His fitters are already trained in plumbing and electrical work
He cannot afford to hold much imported stock
questions.why: Weaknesses are internal and harmful. The stock limit is inside the firm. The bills point is an opportunity, the rival's offer is a threat, and the fitters' skills are a strength.

questions.q: Using the weights given, which option does the matrix favour?
o: Security cameras, with a score of 6.9
Solar water heaters, with a score of 6.9
Solar water heaters, with a score of 6.4
Security cameras, with a score of 7.2
questions.why: Solar: 8×0.4 + 6×0.3 + 7×0.2 + 5×0.1 = 3.2 + 1.8 + 1.4 + 0.5 = 6.9. Cameras: 2.4 + 2.1 + 1.6 + 0.7 = 6.8. The gap is small, so he should test the demand before relying on the score.

questions.q: How should the J$240,000 a month of repair work that his fitters would miss be treated?
o: As a sunk cost that has already been spent
As a fixed cost of the repair business, so it can be ignored
As an opportunity cost to set against the solar income
As a variable cost of each heater he fits
questions.why: It is the benefit he gives up by using the fitters on solar work instead, which is the definition of opportunity cost. It must be set against the extra income when deciding.

questions.q: Which check must Kenroy make before he starts selling and fitting the heaters?
o: The licensing and safety rules for the work
Which colour of van will suit the new service
Whether a trade mark is held by a firm abroad
How much his rival charges for security cameras
questions.why: A new activity may need approvals, and fitting electrical and plumbing equipment has safety rules. Confirm them with the responsible agencies before spending on stock.

questions.q: By what percentage are Anya's weekly pick-ups below her target?
questions.why: Shortfall = 30 − 21 = 9 pick-ups. As a share of the target, 9 ÷ 30 = 30%. Dividing by the actual figure (9 ÷ 21 = 43%) is a common mistake.

questions.q: Guest houses have asked for ironing and folding. What is the best response?
o: Close the service because sales are below the target
Cut the price of the pick-up to attract more guest houses
Wait until the six-month mark and then decide
Test the add-on with a few guest houses and price it
questions.why: Customers asking for a related service is a signal to adjust or pivot. A small test shows whether it pays before she commits. Closing or waiting passively ignores the evidence.

questions.q: Anya wants to stop at week 12. What should she do?
o: Stop now, because sales are 30% below the target
Keep to the exit point and keep testing changes
Raise the target so that the results look better
Continue for a year whatever the weekly sales are
questions.why: Weekly sales of 21 × 9,000 = J$189,000 are above the J$150,000 exit point. The exit point was set to stop emotion deciding, so she tests changes and reviews at six months.
